255.history: The fortified city on the crooked hill commands the roads south of the capital. Its rope-walks, which had spun cable for the fishing boats, turned wholly to winding-rope for the pit-heads in the thirty-first year, and the town grew by half on A' Chompanaidh's pay. A barracks was built there in the years of the constables. When Ashdown's column fell back through it after the ford at Àth chiar, the town shut its gates on the soldiers in the barracks and kept the column's wounded to nurse or to bury. Its citadel commands the roads south of the capital, and the barracks it housed were empty at the close of the age.
255.known_for: winding-rope, and the gates shut on Ashdown

462.history: The walled seat of the eastern mining district was walled by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach after the strikes. Its custodian Coinneach Ruadh signed An Dàrna Athchuinge in the hundred and thirty-ninth year and was turned out of his clerkship at A' Chompanaidh's store within the week, in front of the queue for the week's flour; he was one of eleven who signed and lost A' Chompanaidh's work for it, and he rode the district roads with news for the rest of the age. Its post as custodian Coinneach Ruadh kept eleven years before the petition, and he went on keeping it after he lost the clerkship.

491.history: The mill town a short way from Cill ghlas was where Griogair mac Aonghais told Fearchar Bard to sing the song that went round every pit of the hills without his name on it. In the three years before the rising the smith Uilleam Gobha turned A' Chompanaidh's blasting-powder, bought a keg at a time on a chit of A' Chompanaidh, into bombs packed in tin from the coal sheds' scrap, and forged pike-heads by day out of rail-iron; the rebels' council wrote that without his forge the rising could not have been fought past its first weeks. Taigh na Fèithe above the town kept Leabhar a' Chùraim of the hill through the long centuries, and its keepers set down A' Chompanaidh's coming in the same hand as everything before it.

24.history: The largest of the three towns of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig has been a hawk town since the second house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig was founded there. When Lisle opened a customs house in a hired loft by its fish-steps in the forty-second year, its fishwives chased the officer out twice in his first year, and the roll says only that he went away by water. In the fever years its hawk-faithful raised a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall itself, in open sight of the customs house. It shares its bay with Seann Skell and Ros leathan and has quarrelled with them over moorings for as long as the rolls run.
24.known_for: the customs officer who went away by water

12.history: The ford town of the south-eastern hills, at the meeting of the Abhainn gheal and the Abhainn bhàn, sent its boatmen's sons as runners for Faire nan Lòchran in the years before the war, boys of twelve and thirteen who carried the letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town along the causeway paths, too young for the constables to stop and too quick for a mounted man to follow. It has been a river landing since An Aois Naomh, and its boatmen's causeway paths across the flood-meadows are known to no map.

395.history: The granary of the east keeps the shared-meal custom of An Aois Naomh. In the years before the war Faire nan Lòchran's ledgers of the money it had from Comann an Airgid were kept in the roof-space of its shrine, above the rafters, and no clerk of A' Chompanaidh ever thought to look for them there. It is one of the largest settlements on the island though it is still called a field village, and its grain went to the capital in the siege year.
395.known_for: the ledgers in the shrine roof
